title: What entrepreneurship is: the professor's definitions
summary: Entrepreneurship as mindset, skill and behaviour, and the classic definitions: Hitt, Eckhardt and Shane, Davidsson, Bygrave and Hofer.

chunks.heading: Mindset, skill and behaviour
chunks.explanation_md:
The deck opens by placing entrepreneurship in three words: **mindset, skill and behaviour**.

So entrepreneurship is not only a job title or a company. It is a **way of thinking** (mindset), something you can **learn and practise** (skill), and something people **do** (behaviour). The rest of the deck explains what that thinking and doing look like.
chunks.exam_line: Entrepreneurship is a mindset, a skill and a behaviour.

chunks.heading: Opportunity: discovery, evaluation and exploitation
chunks.explanation_md:
Two definitions focus on **opportunities**:

- **Hitt (2001):** *"Identification and exploitation of previously unexploited opportunities."*
- **Eckhardt and Shane (2003, p. 336):** *"the discovery, evaluation, and exploitation of future goods and services ... [by] ... creation or identification of new ends and means previously undetected or unutilized by market participants."*

The slide sums them up: **entrepreneurship is a process of discovery, evaluation and exploitation of opportunities.** Learn those three steps in order.

chunks.heading: Emergence of new ventures
chunks.explanation_md:
Two more definitions focus on **new ventures coming into being**:

- **Davidsson (2005, p. 21):** entrepreneurship is the **processes of emergence of new business ventures**, real or induced, completed as well as terminated, across organizational and business contexts.
- **Bygrave and Hofer (1991, p. 14):** *all the functions, activities, and actions associated with the **perceiving of opportunities** and the **creation of organizations** to pursue them.*

Notice that Davidsson counts ventures that were **terminated** too: the attempt is part of entrepreneurship, not just the success.

questions.stem: Explain the idea that entrepreneurship is a mindset, a skill and a behaviour.
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck opens by describing entrepreneurship in three words rather than as a job title.

- **Mindset:** a way of thinking that looks for opportunities.
- **Skill:** something that can be learned and practised.
- **Behaviour:** something people actually do, step by step.

The vegetables example shows all three: noticing a need for fresh vegetables (mindset), evaluating that people will pay more (skill), and acting by selling packed, hygienic vegetables (behaviour).

So entrepreneurship is a way of thinking and acting, not only owning a company.

rubric.point: Mindset: a way of thinking
Skill: can be learned and practised
Behaviour: what people do
Vegetables example linking thinking to action

questions.stem: What is common to the definitions of entrepreneurship by Hitt (2001) and Eckhardt and Shane (2003)?
questions.model_answer_md:
Both definitions put **opportunities** at the centre of entrepreneurship.

- **Hitt (2001):** identification and exploitation of previously unexploited opportunities.
- **Eckhardt and Shane (2003):** discovery, evaluation and exploitation of future goods and services by creating or identifying new ends and means that market participants had not noticed or used.
- **Common ground:** an opportunity is first found, then judged, then used. The slide sums this up as a process of **discovery, evaluation and exploitation of opportunities**.

So both see entrepreneurship as a process built around opportunities, not around a firm.

rubric.point: Hitt: identification and exploitation of unexploited opportunities
Eckhardt and Shane: discovery, evaluation, exploitation of future goods and services
New ends and means unnoticed by market participants
Summary: process of discovery, evaluation and exploitation

questions.stem: Define entrepreneurship as given by Davidsson (2005). Why does the definition include terminated ventures?
questions.model_answer_md:
Davidsson (2005) defines entrepreneurship through how new ventures come into being.

- **Definition:** the **processes of emergence of new business ventures**.
- **Real or induced:** ventures that actually start, and those that are prompted or induced.
- **Completed as well as terminated:** ventures that make it and ventures that stop.
- **Across organizational and business contexts:** it can happen inside an existing organization or as a new business.

Terminated ventures are included because the attempt to bring a venture into being is itself entrepreneurship, not only the success.

rubric.point: Processes of emergence of new business ventures
Real or induced
Completed as well as terminated
Across organizational and business contexts

questions.stem: What are the different ways in which entrepreneurship has been defined? Discuss the definitions given by different authors in the deck.
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck does not give one definition of entrepreneurship. It builds the idea from several authors, each stressing a different part.

**1. Mindset, skill and behaviour.** The opening slide places entrepreneurship as a way of thinking, something that can be learned, and something people do.

**2. Opportunity view.**
- **Hitt (2001):** identification and exploitation of previously unexploited opportunities.
- **Eckhardt and Shane (2003):** discovery, evaluation and exploitation of future goods and services by creating or identifying new ends and means not yet noticed or used by market participants.
- The slide sums both up: entrepreneurship is a **process of discovery, evaluation and exploitation of opportunities**.

**3. Venture emergence view.**
- **Davidsson (2005):** the processes of emergence of new business ventures, real or induced, completed as well as terminated, across organizational and business contexts.
- **Bygrave and Hofer (1991):** all the functions, activities and actions associated with perceiving opportunities and creating organizations to pursue them.

**Professor's example.** In the vegetables example, the need is fresh vegetables with a short shelf life (discovery), people are ready to pay more despite a maintenance cost (evaluation), and processed, packed, hygienic vegetables sold at a higher price bring profit (exploitation).

**Common thread:** every definition treats entrepreneurship as a **process** that starts with an opportunity and ends in action or a new organization.

In short, the opportunity view tells us what entrepreneurs look for, and the emergence view tells us what they build.

questions.stem: How are the opportunity-based definitions (Hitt; Eckhardt and Shane) different from the venture-emergence definitions (Davidsson; Bygrave and Hofer)?
questions.model_answer_md:
The deck's definitions fall into two groups. One looks at the opportunity; the other looks at the venture or organization that comes out of it.

| Basis | Opportunity-based | Venture-emergence |
|---|---|---|
| Authors | Hitt (2001); Eckhardt and Shane (2003) | Davidsson (2005); Bygrave and Hofer (1991) |
| Focus | Finding and using opportunities | New ventures and organizations coming into being |
| Key words | Identification, discovery, evaluation, exploitation | Emergence, functions, activities, actions, creation of organizations |
| What counts | Previously unexploited opportunities; new ends and means unnoticed by market participants | Ventures real or induced, completed as well as terminated |
| Context | Markets and market participants | Organizational and business contexts |

**Opportunity view:** Hitt calls it identification and exploitation of previously unexploited opportunities. Eckhardt and Shane add evaluation, giving the summary **discovery, evaluation and exploitation**.

**Emergence view:** Davidsson describes processes of emergence of new business ventures and even counts terminated ones. Bygrave and Hofer join both sides: perceiving opportunities **and** creating organizations to pursue them.

**Link between them:** Bygrave and Hofer act as a bridge, since their definition starts with the opportunity and ends with the organization.

So the two groups are not rivals: one describes the start of the process and the other its result.

Discovery, evaluation and exploitation summary
Emergence: Davidsson, ventures completed or terminated
Bygrave and Hofer: perceiving opportunities and creating organizations
